t.3.43.1: Recognizing in the forest that cry of distress as resembling her husband's voice, Sītā said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Go, find out what has happened to Rāghava."
t.3.43.2: My life does not stay in its place, nor does my heart remain steady, for I have heard the loud cry of one who calls out in the utmost distress.
t.3.43.3: You ought to rescue your brother who is crying out in the forest. Run to him quickly, to your brother who is seeking refuge.
t.3.43.4: "Go to him who has fallen into the power of the Rākṣasas, like a bull fallen into the power of lions!" But though he was spoken to in this way, he did not go, for he heeded his brother's command.
t.3.43.5: Then, there, the angered daughter of Janaka said to him: “Saumitri, in the guise of a friend you are like an enemy to your brother.”
t.3.43.6: You who, in such a situation, do not go to your brother's aid: you wish Rāma to perish, Lakṣmaṇa, for my sake.
t.3.43.7: I think misfortune is dear to you; you have no affection for your brother. That is why you stand here at ease, though you do not see that greatly radiant one.
t.3.43.9: To Vaidehī Sītā, who was speaking thus, overwhelmed with tears and grief, frightened like a young doe, Lakṣmaṇa spoke.
t.3.43.8: For when he has fallen into peril, what could there be for me to do, remaining here, since you, the foremost one, have come here?
t.3.43.11: Even among the fearsome Dānavas, O lovely lady, there could not be found one who would fight back in battle against Rāma, who is equal to Vāsava.
t.3.43.10: O lady, among gods and men, among Gandharvas and birds, among Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Kiṃnaras and beasts alike
t.3.43.12: Rāma cannot be slain in battle; you should not speak thus. I dare not abandon you in this forest without Rāghava.
t.3.43.13: His might cannot be withstood even by the forces of the mighty, nor even by the three worlds united in effort, together with their lords and with the immortals.
t.3.43.14: Let your heart be at peace; let this anguish be cast aside. Your husband will return swiftly, having slain that finest of deer.
t.3.43.16: O Vaidehī, you have become a trust, placed in my keeping by the great-souled Rāma; O lady of fair hips, I cannot bring myself to abandon you here.
t.3.43.15: That was clearly not his voice, nor was it any divine being; it was the illusion of that rākṣasa, unreal as a city of the gandharvas.
t.3.43.17: And, O auspicious one, we have become the enemies of these night-wanderers through the slaying of Khara, O queen, and on account of the slaughter at Janasthāna.
t.3.43.19: Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, she, enraged and with eyes reddened, spoke harsh words to Lakṣmaṇa, the speaker of truth.
t.3.43.18: In the great forest the Rākṣasas send forth such voices by their craft; violence is their sport, O Vaidehī, and you ought not to worry over it.
t.3.43.20: O ignoble one, merciless in your deeds, cruel one, disgrace to your family! I believe this misfortune is pleasing to you; that is why you speak these words.
t.3.43.21: It is no wonder, Lakṣmaṇa, that such wickedness should be found in rivals like you, cruel men who forever go about in disguise.
t.3.43.22: Utterly wicked as you are, you alone follow Rāma, who is alone in the forest, for my sake, in disguise, or else sent by Bharata.
t.3.43.23: Having taken refuge in my husband Rāma, dark as the blue lotus, with eyes like lotuses, how could I desire some other man?
t.3.43.24: O Saumitri, I will give up my life before your very eyes, there is no doubt. Without Rāma I cannot live upon this earth even for a moment.
t.3.43.25: Thus addressed by Sītā with harsh words that made the hair stand on end, Lakṣmaṇa, master of his senses, joined his palms in reverence and spoke to Sītā.
t.3.43.26: I dare not speak a reply, for you are a deity to me. Yet an improper word is nothing strange among women, O Maithilī.
t.3.43.27: But this is the nature of women, as is seen throughout these worlds: women cast off righteousness, they are fickle and sharp-tongued, and they sow discord.
t.3.43.29: Shame on you! May you perish today, since, owing to your womanly nature and wicked disposition, you suspect me thus, though I stand firm in obedience to my elder's command.
t.3.43.28: Let all the forest-dwellers, standing as witnesses, hear me: though I spoke what is right, I have been addressed by you with harsh words.
t.3.43.30: I shall go where Kākutstha is; may it be well with you, O lovely-faced one. May all the deities of the forest protect you, O large-eyed one.
t.3.43.31: For terrible are the omens that are appearing to me. May I, having returned, see you again together with Rāma!
t.3.43.32: Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, the daughter of Janaka, weeping and bathed in tears, then replied with harsh words.
t.3.43.33: Without Rāma, O Lakṣmaṇa, I shall enter the Godāvarī, or I shall hang myself, or I shall cast away my own body upon some rugged precipice.
t.3.43.34: I would rather drink sharp poison or enter the fire; but I will not touch, even with my foot, any man other than Rāghava.
t.3.43.35: Having thus reviled Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, overwhelmed with sorrow and weeping in her grief, beat her belly with both her hands.
t.3.43.36: Seeing her, wide-eyed, weeping and stricken with distress, the dejected Saumitri tried to console her, but Sītā said nothing at all to that brother of her husband.
t.3.43.37: Then Lakṣmaṇa, self-possessed, saluted Sītā with joined palms and bowed slightly; and looking back again and again at Maithilī, he went toward Rāma.
